requirements.status_reason: The enquiry is specific enough to judge the claim, which cannot be supported: the kidney study addresses a different tissue and question and there is no validation on the target use. Key specifications are still missing, so the assessment is provisional.
requirements.answer: No. The kidney study shows a concept in a different tissue for a different question, and with no tumor, boundary or in vivo validation on your setup it cannot be quoted as proof that the sensor is ready for tumor boundary guidance during surgery. The appropriate next step is a laboratory feasibility study on ex vivo tumor and adjacent normal tissue with histopathology as ground truth, followed by animal or clinical studies under ethics and regulatory approval only if the lab results meet pre-set criteria.

inline.headline: Kidney study is supporting context, not readiness evidence; validate tumor discrimination in the lab first
inline.method: Multi-wavelength NIR diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (the reference concept), tested for tumor versus normal tissue discrimination, optionally paired with a second contrast method
inline.probe: Fixed-geometry contact or near-contact fiber probe with defined source-detector separation, sterile single-use sheath concept, and a reference target for calibration
inline.install: Not yet defined; initial work is bench/ex vivo with a fixed positioning jig so spectra can be co-registered to excised tissue
inline.fiber: Illumination and collection fiber bundle with defined numerical aperture and separation, selected after the penetration depth requirement is known
inline.test_against: Histopathology of co-registered measurement spots on resected tumor and adjacent normal tissue, with blinded analysis
inline.not_final_because: Kidney tissue, the target tissue, the contrast mechanism, boundary accuracy requirements, OR conditions and regulatory pathway are all unvalidated, and no in vivo or tumor-specific data exist for this use.

problems.text: The kidney study does not establish readiness for tumor boundary decisions; spectral contrast in kidney tissue does not transfer to tumor versus normal tissue without new data.
Quoting a different-tissue study as proof of readiness would misrepresent the evidence to customers, regulators or surgeons; claims must match the validated scope.
LED NIR diffuse reflectance is largely sensitive to bulk optical properties (blood, water, lipid, scattering); a boundary contrast is not guaranteed and must be measured.
Confounders such as blood content, perfusion, cautery, moisture, probe pressure and ambient OR light may mimic or mask tumor signal and need explicit testing.
Penetration depth of NIR light (typically millimetres) may be insufficient or may sample underlying normal tissue, which limits boundary accuracy at the surface.
Sterility, single-use probe design and calibration stability during surgery are not addressed by the kidney study and affect feasibility.

methods.why: This is the reference concept and the lowest-cost path to test whether tumor and normal tissue show a measurable spectral difference in your own setup.

methods.method: Fluorescence spectroscopy (autofluorescence or with an approved agent)
methods.why: Fluorescence is often more specific for tumor boundaries than reflectance, especially with an agent such as ICG or 5-ALA, but it needs an agent and its own validation.
Gives molecular specificity that reflectance lacks, but signals are weak and acquisition times may be too long for real-time surgical use.
Useful if the surgeon needs a spatial map rather than point readings, but adds complexity; consider only after point-measurement feasibility is shown.
Not practical for in-situ surgical guidance; the tissue is too thick and access is one-sided.

questions.q: Which tumor types and organs are the target, and which tissue will be used as normal reference?
questions.why: Optical properties and contrast differ strongly between tissues, so the validation plan depends on the target.

questions.q: Is a fluorescent or other contrast agent acceptable, or must the method be label-free?
questions.why: This decides whether reflectance alone is feasible or fluorescence/Raman must be added.

questions.q: What boundary accuracy (mm) and decision time are required?
questions.why: These set the required sensitivity, spatial resolution, and acquisition speed, and define go/no-go criteria.

questions.q: What penetration depth must be detected, and can the probe contact the tissue surface?
questions.why: NIR penetration is limited; depth and contact geometry determine whether the sensor can see the tumor margin at all.

questions.q: What did the kidney study report: species, sample size, statistics, and any tumor or boundary data?
questions.why: Any claim must be scoped to what the study actually measured, and gaps must be stated explicitly.

questions.q: What is the intended regulatory status and planned route to clinical use?
questions.why: Research use only, a clinical investigation, and a CE or FDA device pathway require different evidence and risk management (for example ISO 14971 and IEC 60601).

questions.q: Are resected tumor and paired normal tissue specimens available through an ethics-approved pathway?
questions.why: Ex vivo specimens are the most efficient first validation step and avoid premature in vivo work.

experiment.objective: Determine whether the proposed LED NIR probe measurement discriminates tumor from adjacent normal tissue ex vivo on the own setup, with histopathology as ground truth, and decide whether in vivo work is justified.
steps: Define the claim, target tissue, required accuracy, and go/no-go criteria in a written protocol before measuring.
Obtain ethics approval and resected tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens with pathology reports.
Characterise the setup: calibration with reference targets, fixed probe geometry, dark and white references, repeatability and drift over time.
Measure co-registered spots on each specimen with blinded labelling; mark spots and fix them for histology sectioning.
Test confounders: blood or saline overlay, moisture, probe pressure, and ambient light similar to OR lighting.
Analyse spectra with pre-specified features and a classifier using cross-validation and a patient-level held-out set; report sensitivity, specificity, AUC and confidence intervals.
Compare results with histology-based margin assessment and quantify boundary error in mm.
If criteria are met, plan an in vivo animal or first-in-human feasibility study under ethics and regulatory approval, with a risk file under ISO 14971.
If criteria are not met, document the limitations and consider a second modality (fluorescence or Raman) before redesign.
references: ISO 14971 (application of risk management to medical devices)
IEC 60601 series (medical electrical equipment safety and performance)
ISO 10993 (biological evaluation of medical devices), relevant if the probe contacts tissue
Published guidance on diffuse reflectance spectroscopy optical property modelling and on fluorescence-guided surgery, to be selected by the project team
The supplied LED NIR kidney study, for scope and methods only
experiment.go_no_go: Go to in vivo work only if, on independent held-out specimens with histopathology ground truth, discrimination meets pre-specified thresholds (for example AUC and sensitivity/specificity with confidence-interval lower bounds set by the team before testing), boundary error is within the pre-specified mm tolerance, and confounders do not remove the signal. No-go or redesign if these criteria are not met. Thresholds must not be adjusted after data are seen.

multispectral.combination: Multi-wavelength NIR diffuse reflectance as the baseline, combined with fluorescence (autofluorescence or an approved agent) and/or point Raman for molecular specificity, compared on the same specimens.
multispectral.why: Reflectance captures bulk tissue optical differences cheaply but may not separate tumor from normal tissue alone; a second, more specific contrast can confirm or reject boundary decisions and clarifies which signal carries the information.

assumptions: The kidney study is an accurate summary of the supplied document and its tissue and sample details are unknown to this assessment.
No contrast agent is assumed; if one is permitted, fluorescence becomes a stronger candidate.
The intended use is intraoperative guidance, not diagnosis, so a clinical claim requires regulatory evidence beyond feasibility work.
Ex vivo specimens are assumed available through ethics approval; in vivo work is out of scope until the lab study is complete.
Operating-room conditions (ambient light, cautery, bleeding) are not yet specified and are treated as risks to test.
